tags.inscription: Monnow Bridge built circa 1270, as a town defence, is the only surviving medieval bridge in Britain with the gate tower standing on the bridge. The gatehouse has served as a toll-house, guard room, gaol and dwelling house.
tags.inscription:cy: Pont Mynwy. Codwyd Pont Mynwy tua 1270 i warchod y dref. Hi yw'r unig bont o'r canoloesoedd, â phorthdy arni, sydd ar ôl ym Mhrydain. Bu'r porthdy yn ei dro yn dollborh, gwarchodfa, carchar a chartref.
tags.name: Monnow Bridge
tags.operator: Monmouth Civic Society; Monmouth Town Council

tags.inscription: Roman Fort. The defences of Monmouth's 1st century Roman Fort lie under this building - at right angles to the street; the fort pre-dated the Roman town of Blestium.
tags.inscription:continued: The western inner defences of the 11th century Norman town also pass under the building, but diagonally.
tags.inscription:cy: Caer Rufeinig. Mae amddiffyniadau Caer Rufeinig Trefynwy, o'r ganrif 1af, o dan yr adeilad hwn, yn gyfongl i'r stryd. Yn dilyn y gaer, sefydlwyd Blestium, y dref Rufeinig.
tags.inscription:cy:continued: Yma hefyd y claddwyd amddiffyniadau mewnol gorllewinol y dre Normanaidd, yn yr 11 ganrif, ond yn groes-gongl.
tags.name: Roman Fort
tags.operator: Monmouth Civic Society; Monmouth Town Council

tags.inscription: St Mary's Priory Church was dedicated in 1101 by Bernard, Chaplain to Henry I, in the presence of Gwethenoc, the founder, and Abbot William of Saumur in Anjou. The church was rebuilt in 1882, retaining Norman remains and the 14th century tower.
tags.inscription:cy: Cysegrwyd Eglwys Priordy'r Santes Fair yn 1101 gan Bernard, Caplan Harri'r 1af, gyda Gwethenoc, y sylfaenydd, a'r Abad Gwilym o Saumur yn bresennol. Ailgodwyd yr Eglwys yn 1882, gan gadw y twr, o'r 14eg ganrif, a'r olion Normanaidd.
tags.name: St Mary's Priory Church

tags.inscription: The Angel Inn. This site began life as Robert le Ffrere's shop around 1240. For the next 400 years it had various uses, becoming the church brew house by 1613.
tags.inscription:continued: From about 1700 it became The Angel Inn until 1965 when it was returned to its former use as a shop.
tags.inscription:cy: Tafarn yr Angel. Oddeutu 1240 dyma lle'r oedd siop Robert de Ffrere. Yn ystod y 400 mlynedd ganlynol fe'i defnyddiwyd ar gyfer nifer o ddibenion ac yn 1613 dyma lle'r oedd bragdy'r eglwys. O tua 1700 ymlaen dyma lle'r oedd Tafarn yr Angel.
tags.name: The Angel Inn
tags.operator: Monmouth Civic Society; Monmouth Town Council

tags.inscription: The Robin Hood Inn is one of Monmouth's oldest buildings. Its restored front doorway dates from the 16th century, and some interior features from the 17th century.
tags.inscription:continued: In the 18th century, before Catholic emancipation, an upper room here was used to celebrate Mass.
tags.inscription:cy: Tafarn Robin Hood. Dyma un o'r adeiladau hynaf yn Nhrefynwy. Mae'r drws blaen, sydd wedi ei atgyweirio, yn dyddio o'r 16 ganrif, a rhai o'r nodweddion mewnol o'r 17 ganrif.
tags.inscription:cy:continued: Yn y 18 ganrif, cwn Rhyddfreinio'r Papyddion, defnyddiwyd uwch ystafell yn y fan hon i weinyddu'r offeren.
tags.name: The Robin Hood Inn
tags.operator: Monmouth Civic Society; Monmouth Town Council

tags.inscription: The Savoy Theatre occupies what has been called the oldest theatre site in Wales, dating back to Elizabethan times. In 1927 the building was restored and opened as 'The New Picture House' , and the first talking picture was shown in 1930.
tags.inscription:cy: Theatr y Savoy. Mae'n debyg fod theatr wedi sefyll yma, y safle hynaf i theatr yng Nghymru, ers ddyddiau Elizabeth 1af. Fe'i hadferwyd yn 1927 gan ailagor fel 'The New Picture House', ac yno, yn 1930, dangoswyd y ffilm llafar cyntaf.
tags.name: The Savoy Theatre

tags.inscription:1: IN MEMORY OF THE 417 PERSONS KILLED IN THE WORLD WAR II BAEDEKER RAIDS OF 1942  In 1936, Bath City Council demolished 1-3 James Street West in order to build its much-needed council department building, a brand new Labour Exchange. From this building, the
tags.inscription:10: and materials were both in very short supply.
tags.inscription:2: council assisted those seeking employment and paid out subsistence money ("the dole") to those in need from 1937 onwards. When World War II broke out in 1939 its function was extended to include civil defence. On 26th April 1942, in the early hours of the
tags.inscription:3: morning, a 250kg bomb hit the Holy Trinity Church just 40 metres west of this site. Shrapnel from the wrecked church caused minor damage to the outside of the Labour Exchange. At approximately the same time the next morning another bomb landed on the edge
tags.inscription:4: of the pavement on the north side of James Street West, opposite the Kingsmead North junction.  Wartime records show that the new Labour Exchange was badly damaged by this second blast. The building was immediately evacuated and the fire service worked
tags.inscription:5: through the night, using more than ten pumps, to make the area safe. Despite their efforts the fire in the roof spread and burned out the whole of the top floor. It was recorded that the stone of the building was left severely pitted by shrapnel and
tags.inscription:6: machine gun fire, and the damage can still be seen on the retained façade of the building.  Despite the building being severely damaged, the funcitons carried out there were still badly needed. The floor of the upper storey was hastily sealed to make a
tags.inscription:7: temporary roof and the hole in the outside wall patched with cement. Thus the Labour Exchange continued to operate from the stump of the original building, providing essential support for those bombed out of their homes and ensuring that the war effort
tags.inscription:8: had sufficient manpower.  This became even more important when wartime emergency legislation made it compulsory for all unmarried women to be employed on functions that assisted the war effort and the Labour Exchange had to help them find suitable jobs.
tags.inscription:9: For a long period after the war the Labour Exchange was used solely for storage but in 2002 it was designated as a Grade II listed building because it was one of the last surviving examples of the "make do and mend" necessities of wartime, when manpower
tags.name: Bath Blitz information plaque
